rv.q: The revival of Dames At Sea that opened on Broadway Thursday night is a lot of fun and a tribute to the city’s inexhaustible pool of inexhaustible talent, if not actual stars.
There’s nothing wrong with this revival that Peters, who played the role of Ruby in the original 1968 production, couldn’t fix.
Nothing whatsoever to dislike—but there isn't enough to love about 'Dames at Sea.'

Dames at Sea reinvents one of those big-screen spectacles as a shrunken stage musical — a baby Busby Berkeley if you will — with an appealing cast of six that makes its featherweight pleasures infectious.

Nearly 50 years on, however, with Broadway having thoroughly strip-mined the songs and styles of the shows that made up the so-called Golden Age of the musical, the little show that could, and did, seems to give off a faint whiff of mothballs.
In the end, no such luck: pfffffft.
What the musical does not have -- in addition to a breakout ingénue to elevate the unrelentingly, cheerfully lame nonsense -- is charm.
But pumping up the material for Broadway another 50 years along has turned it leaden and charmless.
It's not funny enough to be satire and yet too earnest to be believed.

"The classic all talking, all dancing, all singing, all sassy pastiche of the 1930 film musicals is back and worthy of a twenty-one gun salute... The principal creative force behind this revival is Randy Skinner.
For lovers of the genre, Dames at Sea is a delightful romp that doesn't feel like it's aged a day since 1966.
This charming little show is a star bright enough to outshine some of its flashier neighbors on the Great White Way.
Randy Skinner's tap-happy production delivers plenty of sly amusement thanks to a ferociously talented sextet of triple threats.
It’s delightful, and it doesn’t take itself seriously for a minute.

Dames at Sea Theatre Review by Matthew Murray - October 22, 2015. Dames at Sea Book and lyrics by George Haimsohn and Robin Miller. Music by Jim Wise. Directed and choreographed by Randy Skinner. Music supervision, vocal and dance arrangements by Rob Berman. Orchestrations by Jonathan Tunick. Scenic design by Anna Louizos. Costume design by David C.
This Dames at Sea has merriment, heart, and plenty of sparkle.
A show doesn't have to be a masterpiece to provide an enjoyable evening of theater.
When the decidedly minor "Beguine" in the second act literally stops Dames at Sea in its tracks, you know that something is off kilter.
It's a fun, family-friendly musical that will be a holiday season crowd-pleaser.
I suggest those who love lots of tap dancing, old-fashioned tunes, and a touch of camp get down to the Theatre on the double.
For a pleasant two hour visit with a score that never even tries to be original, and with six eager and talented singers-dancers-actors, you can have a jolly time at the Theatre.
Never mind; just check your cares and pretensions at the door of the Theatre, where this production opened Thursday, and prepare to be thoroughly charmed.
Dames at Sea, for its innocuous delights, is a perfectly happy theatrical entry, but perhaps it has spent fifty years off Broadway for a reason: its satire does not bite so much as nibble.
It arrives as an example of how dated material can still entertain when blessed with a cast and crew of talented professionals.
Without that, the experience becomes a series of individual numbers rather than a satisfyingly cohesive whole.
To the extent that it delivers on its marketing hype, Dames at Sea largely loses what made it distinctive in the first place.
Before long, though, monotony sets in and won't go away.
Dames at Sea offers a few nostalgic chuckles, but it's hard to see what it's doing on Broadway.
Otherwise "Ripcord" aims too low and still barely delivers.
It’s not fun to feel superior to such material; it’s numbing.
Alas, Dames at Sea isn't big enough — or good enough — to command a Broadway stage, even at the diminutive Helen Hayes.
At my performance, I wanted to shout back at them, “Calm down. You’re not making the situation any better.”
By jettisoning the original light production values that delighted critics and audiences at the time this Dames at Sea sinks under the weight of its contemporary trappings.
Dames at Sea is a very funny and witty diversion of a show and should be seen by anyone who just wants to spend a few hours in a theater.
This production acts as a refreshing, laugh-out-loud contemporary companion to the shows from the era it's set in.
Fun, fun, fun, and definitely recommended.
With that in mind, I recommend you set sail for Dames at Sea, now at the Theatre.
If you let it entertain you, you'll have a real good time.
As for Dames at Sea, it may have a rough time staying afloat on the Great White Way.
But, alas, it seems the magic has gone.

cn.t: Critics are divided on this featherweight 1960s spoof of 1930s movie musicals, praising the energetic tap dancing and hardworking cast but questioning whether the dated material belongs on Broadway at all.

sg.ra: Multiple guides converge on Rows B to H center as the best views in Broadway's smallest house (597 seats), where the intimate scale means these seats feel closer to the stage than premium orchestra in any other Broadway theater. The Hayes-specific tradeoff: patrons repeatedly flag that the stage sits unusually high for such an intimate room, so Row A and the very front can force neck-craning — one AVFMS viewer described the Hayes stage as 'particularly high for the first couple of rows, so you'll be using your neck to look up,' and a JOB patron noted 'The stage is high so you don't see actors' feet.' Rows B-H sit far enough back to clear that stage-height issue while still letting you read facial expressions in a house this small.

sg.vl: Value sweet spot where the rake kicks in
sg.ra: Rows F-M center are consistently flagged as the value band at Hayes — priced below premium but still close in a 597-seat room. The Hayes-specific reason to favor the back half of that band (J-M) over F-I: an AVFMS reviewer explicitly observed that 'Row J in the orchestra level is where the rake of the floor starts to increase so even a short guy like me can see over someone tall.' That makes J-M the first rows where a tall head in front stops being a problem, which matters more at Hayes than at larger houses because the orchestra is 'more long than it is wide' (NYTix) and the stage height is tall, so front-orchestra sightlines are flatter than usual.

The very back row of the Hayes mezzanine sits directly against the theater's staff/operations area — a quirk specific to this post-2018-renovation layout. Multiple AVFMS reviewers independently complain the ushers or crew are audible throughout the show from Mezz Row J: one wrote 'this row butts up against the row where the theater staff sits and they chatted, loudly, throughout the show'; another said 'the ushers downstairs were loud and I could sometimes hear their murmurings'; an accessible-seat user at Mezz J-101 reported 'there's some sort of operation booth to the right of this seat and it's very loud and distracting. I could hear talking and typing throughout the entire show.' Because Hayes is the smallest house on Broadway, there's no orchestra noise to mask ambient staff chatter the way a 1,500-seat venue would — in this intimate room, the booth chatter carries.
